newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Seoul plans further financial markets deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Seoul plans further financial markets deregulation.

text.p: South Korea is on track to further deregulate its financial markets in preparation for joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the head of Seoul's stock exchange said on Friday.

"We will further deregulate the markets. We will also raise the foreign ceiling for equities by three percent every year from 1997 and abolish it by the year 2000," Hong In-kie, chairman of the Korea Stock Exchange, told Reuters in an interview.
As of October 1, foreign investors can buy up to 20 percent of total shares in each listed company with an individual ceiling of five percent.
Hong said since the limit was established, over $600 million in fresh funds had flowed into the market.
Until now, about $16 billion had been invested in the stock market and foreign ownership had reached 13 percent of total market capitalisation, he said.
Hong said this measure and others were the results of Seoul's proposed entry into the OECD group of wealthy nations. South Korea was invited last week to join the Paris-based club.
"South Korea will be a ceilingless country in the year 2000," Hong said, adding that the bond market would also be opened soon.
The South Korean bond market was initially opened in July, 1995, to foreigners on a limited basis only.
They were allowed to invest in convertible bonds issued by small and medium-sized companies.
Hong, who was attending a World Bank and Asian Developemnt Bank conference in Bali, Indonesia, said South Korea planned to allow international participation in the bond market.
"This is to show our commitment we made to the OECD."

But Hong did not give firm dates for opening the stock and bond markets. Han Seung-soo, Minister of Finance and Economy, said earlier foreign investors would be allowed to invest in convertible and straight bonds issued by large companies in 1998 and 1999.

South Korea had been pressed by OECD members to speed up liberalisation of its financial markets as the price for membership. But the government had resisted radical reforms and accepted only part of the liberalisation code.
South Korea applied for OECD membership in March 1995. It will be the second Asian OECD member after Japan.
Hong said foreign brokerage firms would also be allowed to increase their share in joint ventures in the local securities industry.
Currently, foreign parties can only hold less than a 50 percent stake in a stock brokerage firm.
"Higher foreign ownership might be permissible in the near future," Hong said, adding that competition would be tougher for South Korean companies following the entry into OECD.
But he said interest rates might fall in the medium-term, which should help boost the stock market further.
"Interest rates are in a downtrend. Yields on corporate bonds have declined to 11 percent from 13 percent," Hong said.
He said the government had recently announced a package of policies to enhance national competitiveness by 10 percent, including lowering interest rates to a single digit.
Hong said the government also planned to open the mutual funds market to foreigners. Currently only South Koreans are allowed to set up mutual funds.
